extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and instructors in dynamical systems / applied mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, criteria, and worked examples for chaotic behavior in one-dimensional discrete dynamical systems (logistic map, doubling map, tent map), symbolic dynamics, and the Cantor set. Includes constructions, theorems, and experimental exploration instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of chaos for interval maps
rubrics_metrics.description: A map f that takes an interval I = [α, β] to itself is chaotic if (1) periodic points of f are dense in I; (2) f is transitive on I (given any two subintervals U1 and U2 in I, there is a point x0 ∈ U1 and an n > 0 such that f^n(x0) ∈ U2); (3) f has sensitive dependence in I (there is a sensitivity constant β such that, for any x0 ∈ I and any open interval U about x0, there is some seed y0 ∈ U and n > 0 such that |f^n(x0) − f^n(y0)| > β).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that, for maps of an interval, condition (3) is redundant (the first two topological conditions imply sensitivity). It also remarks that transitivity is equivalent to the existence of a dense orbit (dense orbit ⇒ transitivity is clear; the converse uses the Baire Category Theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic points are dense (criterion/implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic points of f are dense in I: in every subinterval of I there exists a periodic point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the first condition in the definition of chaos. Demonstrated explicitly for the doubling map by showing D^n crosses the diagonal in each subinterval [k/2^n, (k+1)/2^n], hence a periodic point in each such interval; lengths 1/2^n → 0 so periodic points are dense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological transitivity (criterion/implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: f is transitive on I: given any two subintervals U1 and U2 in I, there exists x0 ∈ U1 and n > 0 with f^n(x0) ∈ U2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent (for interval maps) to the existence of an orbit that is dense in I. Used as the second condition in the definition of chaos; demonstrated for the doubling map by showing some iterate maps small dyadic intervals to the whole interval [0,1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (criterion/implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a sensitivity constant β > 0 such that for any x0 ∈ I and any neighborhood U of x0, there is y0 ∈ U and n > 0 with |f^n(x0) − f^n(y0)| > β.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third condition of chaos. For the doubling map one may choose β = 1/2. For f4 (logistic at λ=4) the text shows β = 1/2 works via semi-conjugacy with the tent map; for the shift map the maximal sensitivity constant 2 can be chosen. Note: for interval maps this property follows from the first two (redundant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugacy between interval maps
rubrics_metrics.description: f : I → I and g : J → J are conjugate if there is a homeomorphism h : I → J such that h ∘ f = g ∘ h.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conjugacy takes orbits of f to orbits of g (h(f^n(x)) = g^n(h(x))). Conjugacy preserves chaotic behavior on closed finite-length intervals: if f is chaotic on I then g is chaotic on J. Example: f4 (4x(1−x)) is conjugate to g(x)=x^2−2 via a specific affine h, so chaoticity transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semi-conjugacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous function h that is at most n-to-one and satisfies f ∘ h = h ∘ g is called a semi-conjugacy between g and f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A semi-conjugacy also preserves chaotic behavior on intervals of finite length (though it need not preserve minimal periods of cycles; it maps cycles to cycles). Example: the tent map T and logistic f4 are semi-conjugate via h(x) = (1 − cos 2πx)/2 (two-to-one except at 1/2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubling map D(x)=2x mod 1 is chaotic (example / constructive criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: D : [0,1) → [0,1) given by D(x)=2x for 0 ≤ x < 1/2 and D(x)=2x−1 for 1/2 ≤ x < 1. For all n, D^n(x) = 2^n x mod 1, so the graph of D^n consists of 2^n straight lines and D^n maps each interval [k/2^n,(k+1)/2^n] onto [0,1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From these facts one deduces periodic points are dense, transitivity holds (any open J contains one such dyadic interval), and sensitivity holds with β = 1/2. The doubling map provides an explicit, fully understandable chaotic example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tent map T is chaotic (continuous cousin example)
rubrics_metrics.description: T(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x < 1/2 and T(x) = −2x + 2 for 1/2 ≤ x ≤ 1. The graphs of T^n show that T acts like the doubling map and is chaotic on [0,1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof follows exactly as in the doubling map case using T^n graphs. The tent map is used to semi-conjugate to f4 and transfer sensitivity constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistic map fixed points and bifurcations (λ-dependent stability)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f_λ(x)=λ x(1−x) on I=[0,1]: f_λ(0)=0 always (fixed). 0 is attracting in I for 0 < λ ≤ 1 and repelling thereafter. f_λ(1)=0 so 1 is eventually fixed. For λ>1 there is a second fixed point x_λ=(λ−1)/λ in I; x_λ is attracting for 1 < λ ≤ 3 and repelling for λ > 3. At λ = 3 a period-doubling bifurcation occurs. For λ between 3 and ≈3.4 the only periodic points present are the two fixed points and a 2-cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These parameter-range statements give precise stability/bifurcation thresholds used to understand routes to chaos (period-doubling cascade). Exercises refer to further classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special structure and chaos at λ = 4 for the logistic map
rubrics_metrics.description: For λ=4, f_4 has a single critical point at 1/2 with f_4(1/2)=1 and f_4^2(1/2)=0, and f_4 maps each half-interval [0,1/2] and [1/2,1] onto the entire interval I. Iterating shows f_4^n has 2^n fixed points in I (so many periodic points of various periods exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphical iterations of random seeds under f_4 often appear 'chaotic' (orbits look aperiodic); semi-conjugacy with the tent map and conjugacy arguments explain and prove chaoticity of f_4 on the appropriate invariant set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-escaping set for λ>4 and Cantor-like structure (symbolic dynamics setup)
rubrics_metrics.description: For λ>4 the interval I = [0,1] is not invariant: some orbits escape to −∞. Define the nonescaping set Λ (denoted (cid:51) in text) as the set of points in I with orbits that never leave I. There exists an open exit interval A0 where f_λ > 1 so points in A0 escape; define An as preimages producing 2^n disjoint open intervals; Λ = I  igcup_{n≥0} An is a Cantor-set-like set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition I  ackslash A0 into two closed intervals I0 (left) and I1 (right). Points in Λ have entire orbits in I0 ∪ I1, allowing an itinerary of 0s and 1s to be associated to each nonescaping point. This sets up symbolic dynamics on Λ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Itinerary function S and symbolic coding of orbits
rubrics_metrics.description: Given x0 in the nonescaping set Λ, associate an infinite sequence S(x0) = (s0 s1 s2 ...) with sj = k iff f_λ^j(x0) ∈ I_k (k = 0 or 1). S(x0) is called the itinerary of x0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The itinerary provides a map S : Λ → Σ (Σ = {0,1}^N). Under suitable conditions on λ (text: λ sufficiently large; λ > 2 + sqrt(5) is a sufficient condition noted), S is one-to-one, onto, continuous with continuous inverse (a homeomorphism). The nested-interval construction Is0...sn shows existence/uniqueness of x for any admissible finite block and yields S being a homeomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric on the sequence space Σ = {0,1}^N
rubrics_metrics.description: Define d(s,t) = sum_{i=0}^∞ |s_i − t_i| / 2^i for sequences s=(s0s1...) and t=(t0t1...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This series converges (numerators are 0 or 1) and defines a metric on Σ. Useful propositions: if s_j = t_j for j = 0,...,n then d(s,t) ≤ 1/2^n; conversely if d(s,t) < 1/2^n then s_j = t_j for j = 0,...,n. These facts are used to prove continuity of the itinerary map and shift map.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift map σ on Σ and its dynamical properties
rubrics_metrics.description: σ(s0 s1 s2 ...) = (s1 s2 s3 ...). σ is continuous and two-to-one onto Σ (σ(0 s) = σ(1 s)). Periodic points of period n are exactly the sequences formed by repeating a block of length n; fixed points are (0) and (1), 2-cycles are (01) and (10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct explicit sequences with dense orbit (concatenation of all finite blocks) to show σ is transitive; sensitivity constant can be chosen as 2 (maximal distance). σ is therefore chaotic and serves as a completely understandable model for f_λ on Λ via conjugacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugacy between f_λ on Λ and the shift map σ via itinerary S
rubrics_metrics.description: The itinerary function S : Λ → Σ provides a conjugacy between f_λ on Λ and σ, i.e., S ∘ f_λ = σ ∘ S (under the hypotheses where S is a homeomorphism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because S is a homeomorphism and satisfies S(f_λ(x)) = σ(S(x)), chaoticity of σ transfers to f_λ on Λ. This gives a computable symbolic model for f_λ's dynamics on the nonescaping Cantor-like set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor middle-thirds set: construction and address coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct C by iteratively removing the open middle third of each closed interval: after n stages there are 2^n closed intervals of length 1/3^n; C is the limit set. Attach an address of L/R at each stage (or equivalently digits 0/2) to each point in C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points in C correspond to ternary expansions containing only 0s and 2s (endpoints have dual representations, one containing a 1). C is uncountable, has the same cardinality as [0,1], and has Lebesgue measure (length) 0. The address coding gives a natural homeomorphism between the nonescaping set Λ (for certain f_λ) and C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orbit-diagram experimental procedure (practical exploration rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct an orbit diagram for f_λ(x)=λ x(1−x) by choosing N equally spaced λ-values in [0,4], computing the orbit of 0.5 under f_λj for each λ_j, and plotting points (λ_j, f_λj^k(0.5)) for k in some tail-range (e.g., 50 ≤ k ≤ 250), thereby displaying the fate of the orbit of 0.5 across parameter values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical recommended parameters: N=800 with λ_j = 0.005 j; plot the last 200 iterates over each λ_j. Suggested investigations: behavior in the 'period 1 window' 0 ≤ λ < 3.57..., period-doubling bifurcations, causes of smeared regions near bifurcations, investigation of the 'period 3 window' (~3.828–3.857), arrangement and self-similarity of period-n windows, interpretation of darker curves (higher density of plotted orbit points).
